title: Reply: sufficiency is of Scripture's body taken indefinitely, not of every booklet
source_text: III. Respondeo, quum dicimus Scripturam sufficienter continere omnia necessaria, nos id non intelligere de singulis Scripturae libris, quasi nullus esset Scripturae libellus in quo non traderentur omnia fidei dogmata. Sed hoc verum esse de Scripturae corpore indefinite sumpto, & secundum partes saltem praecipuas. Dico autem notanter de Scripturae corpore indefinite sumpto, & secundum partes praecipuas, quia mens nostra non est, doctrinam necessariam ita in toto Scripturae corpore contineri, ut, si inde pars aliqua, & liber aliquis dematur, statim aliquid desit ad integritatem doctrinae, quod in argumento supponunt adversarii. Nam in Scripturae corpore, prout illud hodie habemus, doctrina salutis continetur non tantum sufficienter, sed etiam abundanter. Suntque plures Scripturae libri in quibus nova dogmata non traduntur, & diversa ab iis quae alibi docentur, sed tantum luculentiores quaedam eorundem dogmatum explicationes & applicationes, sive ad contrarios errores refutandos, sive ad mores hominum formandos & instituendos. Itaque absque doctrinae salutaris dispendio quibusdam Scripturae sacrae libris carere possemus, & qui Ecclesiae dati sunt, non precise ad necessitatem, verum ad ubertatem & majorem utilitatem. Quamvis ergo daremus scripta quaedam divina & authentica periisse, non inde tamen sequeretur integram salutis doctrinam in Scriptura non posse amplius reperiri. Nam fieri posset ut alia quaedam scripta divina extiterint, neque tamen in iis ullum fuerit dogma, sive praeceptum, quod hodie non extet in Scripturae partibus quae supersunt.
pass_a_gloss: I answer: when we say Scripture sufficiently contains all necessary things, we do not understand that of each several book of Scripture, as if there were no little book of Scripture in which all dogmas of faith were not handed down. But this is true of the body of Scripture taken indefinitely, and according to its principal parts at least. I say expressly of the body of Scripture taken indefinitely and according to the principal parts, because it is not our mind that the necessary doctrine is so contained in the whole body of Scripture that if some part, and some book, is taken away, something immediately is wanting to the integrity of the doctrine — which the adversaries' argument assumes. For in the body of Scripture as we have it today, the doctrine of salvation is contained not only sufficiently but even abundantly. And there are several books of Scripture in which new dogmas are not handed down, different from those taught elsewhere, but only certain clearer explanations and applications of the same dogmas, whether for refuting contrary errors or for forming and instructing men's manners. So without loss to saving doctrine we could lack certain sacred books; and those given to the Church were given not precisely for bare necessity, but for abundance and greater usefulness. Even if we granted that certain divine and authentic writings had perished, it would not follow that the whole doctrine of salvation can no longer be found in Scripture. For it could be that certain other divine writings existed, and yet in them there was no dogma or precept which does not still exist today in the parts of Scripture that remain.
pass_b_english: We never meant: every single biblical booklet by itself teaches every dogma.
Sufficiency belongs to Scripture's body taken as a whole — indefinitely, and at least in its chief parts.
Rome assumes that dropping any one book instantly guts doctrine. That is not our claim.
Today's corpus holds salvation's teaching not only enough, but richly; many books only explain or apply what others already teach.
Even if some authentic divine writings had perished, the remaining Scripture could still hold the full saving doctrine — those lost books need not have carried any dogma missing from what survives.
